claims.statement: CEFR is useful as a descriptive communicative-capability framework but is not a teaching algorithm.
A balanced language course should include meaning-focused input, meaning-focused output, language-focused learning and fluency development.
Spacing and repeated retrieval can support second-language vocabulary retention; no single fixed repetition rule is justified for all learners/items.
Captions can function as a scaffold for second-language video learning, but exact support policy should depend on learner/task/outcome.
Lexical knowledge is incremental and task-sensitive; a single binary known/unknown flag is an inadequate representation of observed word or chunk knowledge.
For tested form-meaning and related word-knowledge components, recognition generally precedes or is easier than recall; recognition success therefore does not establish recall ability.
Receptive vocabulary availability can exceed productive availability, so comprehension evidence should not be silently promoted to productive evidence.
The amount and strength of observed vocabulary knowledge depend materially on test format, cueing/scoring choices, and the inference the task is designed to support.
Immediate vocabulary performance does not establish retention; delayed tests often show substantially lower performance than immediate tests.

Adult L2 vocabulary training is stronger when it develops phonological/orthographic/meaning representations and form-meaning connections through retrieval, spacing and/or elaboration rather than massed repetition alone.
Vocabulary research disproportionately measures receptive form-meaning knowledge; success on those tasks should not be interpreted as complete knowledge of form, meaning and use.

Chunk/collocation knowledge requires purpose-matched receptive and productive evidence; partial cues can change the construct being measured and validated productive measures remain comparatively limited.

Several common L2 word-knowledge performances may behave as indicators of one underlying vocabulary-knowledge construct; Nếp evidence categories must not be presented as proven independent psychological dimensions.

At initial learning stages, form-meaning and spoken/written form deserve priority while collocations, multiple meanings, derivatives and constraints on use can deepen progressively rather than being prerequisites for every first exposure.

Strategic multilingual/L1-inclusive instruction can support L2 learning and may outperform monolingual L2-only instruction on average in represented settings, but effects are heterogeneous and intervention quality varies.
For vocabulary meaning support, L1 glosses generally produce equal or greater learning than L2 glosses, with some meta-analytic evidence of a larger relative advantage for beginner learners.
Teacher-provided L1 lexical explanation can produce greater immediate and delayed L2 vocabulary gains than L2 lexical explanation in the synthesized classroom evidence.
Glossing facilitates L2 vocabulary learning, but observed effects depend on test format and other design features; supported recognition cannot be treated as equivalent to independent recall or use.
Current evidence does not justify one universal percentage of L1 use or one fixed vocabulary-count/calendar threshold for removing L1 support.

Lower-proficiency learners often benefit relatively more from L1/gloss support, but moderator findings are not fully consistent across meta-analyses; fading direction is better supported than any exact fading rule.
Long-term effects of broad translanguaging policies are less certain than immediate achievement effects because delayed posttests remain uncommon in the synthesized literature.
Principled L1 inclusion can coexist with development of L2 speaking and writing in beginner instruction; L1 support is not inherently incompatible with productive target-language practice.
When answer-bearing L1 support is visible, the resulting success is scaffolded evidence rather than independent L2 comprehension or recall; support provenance must be part of the interpretation.
The best Vietnamese-specific scaffold sequence and fading threshold for a near-A0 audio-first web learner remain unvalidated product assumptions.

L2 listening performance draws on distinguishable lower-level processes such as input decoding, spoken-word recognition and parsing as well as higher-level meaning/discourse construction; a task should not be assumed to measure all of them equally.

Aural word recognition and decoding are strongly related to listening comprehension but are not identical to message comprehension; successful comprehension can sometimes occur with imperfect word-by-word decoding.
Learners can know lexical items in written form yet fail to recognize the same language in connected speech because spoken-form access, phonological variation and segmentation are additional demands.

Explicit decoding training can improve EFL/ESL listening outcomes; the synthesized decoding literature shows a medium average benefit over non-decoding instruction, while general listening instruction shows a smaller positive pooled effect.

High-variability phonetic training can improve L2 speech perception with evidence of retention and some generalization, but phonetic perception outcomes should not be interpreted as whole-message listening comprehension.

Listening strategy instruction has positive synthesized effects, and one low-proficiency study found an integrated bottom-up plus metacognitive approach more effective than metacognitive instruction alone; bottom-up and higher-level work should be integrated rather than treated as substitutes.
Aural/phonological vocabulary knowledge is important enough to measure separately from written vocabulary when the product claim concerns listening ability.

Transcript/caption visibility changes the information available to the learner and therefore an answer produced with answer-bearing text visible is not equivalent evidence to audio-only listening performance.
Dictation and transcription are useful decoding diagnostics but written response requirements can add orthographic demands, so scoring and task labels must match the intended listening construct.
No universal A0 replay count or word-decoding percentage for declaring listening comprehension was established by this research cycle.

Spaced practice improves second-language learning relative to massed practice on average; longer spacing is more likely to show an advantage on delayed rather than immediate tests, so interval quality must be judged against the intended retention horizon.

The L2 literature does not establish expanding spacing as universally superior to equal spacing; the strongest synthesis found them statistically equivalent overall while individual studies vary with spacing amount and retention interval.

Additional within-session retrievals can raise later vocabulary scores, but the efficiency advantage shrinks when time-on-task is controlled; more repetitions are not automatically better use of learner time.

Retrieval format changes what is learned: recall practice is especially useful when later productive form retrieval is required, whereas recognition can be sufficient for narrower recognition outcomes.

Corrective feedback after a retrieval attempt supports error correction, but L2 evidence does not justify a universal delayed-feedback rule; when lag to test was controlled, immediate versus delayed feedback timing showed little overall difference.

Retrieval practice generally improves later retention relative to restudy, but benefits depend on successful enough retrieval and task conditions; deliberately making retrieval so hard that the learner repeatedly fails is not justified as a default learning policy.

Retrieval practice can support transfer to changed contexts, but transfer effects are conditional and smaller than simple same-task retention; a scheduler event therefore cannot by itself establish transfer.

Data-driven spaced-repetition systems can model recall probability/memory dynamics and optimize review cost from large longitudinal review logs, making adaptive scheduling a defensible engineering strategy for memory review.

FSRS-style scheduler states and predicted retrievability are scheduling estimates, not direct observations of English comprehension, production, transfer or mastery; benchmark accuracy on card recall must not be re-labeled as language-learning efficacy.

No universal review interval, fixed repetition count, desired-retention target or FSRS grade mapping has been validated specifically for Vietnamese-speaking near-A0 Nếp learners across the product's different evidence lanes.

Same-context or same-response retesting supports retention evidence but does not by itself establish transfer; transfer requires a meaningful change in cue, context, exemplar, modality or required response.
Retrieval practice can improve transfer on average, but transfer effects are conditional on the relationship between training and final task and are not equivalent to same-task retention effects.

Experience across varied contexts can support more flexible use of learned word meanings in new contexts, but the strength of this effect depends on learner, task and how contextual diversity is operationalized.

Direct L2 evidence does not support a universal more-contextual-diversity-is-better rule; contextual variation increases processing demand and its benefit can be smaller or adverse for learners with lower lexical proficiency.

High performance in a familiar or repeated context can coexist with weaker performance in an unfamiliar context, so trained-context fluency should not be silently promoted to flexible generalisation evidence.

When the product claim concerns productive use, productive practice and productive probes provide information that receptive recognition tasks cannot substitute for, although productive tasks impose greater time and language demands.

Difficulty during foreign-vocabulary learning can sometimes improve delayed retention or transfer, but difficulty is not universally desirable and can produce interference or failure when foundations are weak.

For a valid changed-context inference, non-target language and answer cues should be controlled so failure is attributable as narrowly as possible to the target capability rather than unrelated novelty.
Once an unseen transfer probe has been attempted, subsequent reuse is no longer first-exposure transfer evidence because testing/retrieval itself can change later learning and retention.

The optimal novelty ladder, probe frequency and cheapest predictive transfer task for Vietnamese-speaking near-A0 Nếp learners are not established by current literature and require product validation.
